voyage.content: Holds regular celebrations of the Catholic Mass

voyage.content: The hosts the Gnostic Mass and frequent classes on Magick; Bywater

voyage.content: Distributes Voodoo goods and holds Voodoo ceremonies in the Marigny

voyage.name: Esoterica
voyage.content: Supplies wares, herbs, and oils in the French Quarter.

voyage.name: Steamboat Natchez Riverboat Harbor Jazz Sightseeing Cruise
voyage.price: Adult/child 6-13/child under 6: daytime cruise $34/13.50/free; M-Sa cruise with lunch $46/23/9.50; Sunday brunch with cruise $51/27.50/17.50; evening cruise $48/24/free; cruise with dinner $83/38/18.25
voyage.hours: Daytime cruise daily 11:30AM and 2:30PM, Mon-Sat evening cruise 7PM
voyage.content: Two-hour cruise on a stream-powered paddlewheel boat. Boarding 30 min before departure (1 hour before dinner cruise). Live narration of historical facts and highlights of the port. Bar and gift shop. Snacks and light meals available for purchase if you're not buying a meal.

voyage.name: Creole Queen Sightseeing Cruise
voyage.price: Daytime: adult $34, child (6-12) $14, child under 6 free; buffet $19 per person, or available à la carte. Evening with dinner/without: adult $79/48, child (6-12) $36/24, child (3-5) $12/free
voyage.hours: Daily: daytime cruise 10AM and 2PM, evening cruise with jazz band 7PM
voyage.content: A diesel-powered paddlewheel boat. A one-hour shore excursion at the battlefield features a guided tour and talk by National Park Rangers. Boarding 30 min before departure.

voyage.name: New Orleans Pedal Barge
voyage.hours: Cruises and tours start at 10am and occur every 2 hours
voyage.content: Pedal a stationary bike around a communal bar that powers a paddlewheel. Up to 18 participants.

voyage.name: Cajun Encounters
voyage.alt: Heading eastbound Highway 90 from the intersection with Highway 190, it is beside the first bridge that you reach (about 1 km east of the intersection)
voyage.price: $32.75 for adults without transportation to swamp, $59.75 for adult including transportation from New Orleans
voyage.content: A two hour flat boat tour involving seeing the swamp, wildlife (e.g. alligators, birds, raccoons), and houses of people living in the swamp lands.

voyage.name: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival
voyage.content: Also known as Jazz Fest. Held the last weekend in April and the first weekend in May every year at the New Orleans Fairgrounds, F-Su 11AM-7PM. It is second only to Mardi Gras for importance and size for New Orleans. The festival has been held every year since 1970. The true heart and soul of the Jazz Fest, as with New Orleans, is music. That includes jazz, both traditional and contemporary, Cajun music, blues, R&B, g

voyage.name: French Quarter Festival
voyage.content: Big free music festival at locations all around the French Quarter each Spring, usually the week before the start of JazzFest.

voyage.name: Essence Festival
voyage.content: Big music festival in the Superdome and Convention Center in early July featuring top R&B, Gospel, and Hip-Hop artists, and a general celebration of contemporary African-American music and culture.

voyage.name: San Fermin in Nueva Orleans
voyage.content: Started as a bit of silliness by a bunch of friends in 2007: The idea was to replicate the famous "running of the bulls" in Pamplona, but with roller-derby girls with plastic baseball bats serving as the "bulls" chasing the runners. It caught on, and now attracts thousands of participants and even more spectators each July in the French Quarter and CBD.

voyage.name: Satchmo Summer Festival
voyage.content: First held in 2001 to mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of New Orleans jazz legend Louis "Satchmo" Armstrong. Organizers were unsure how many people would come out for a music festival in the August heat, but it was such a success that it's been repeated ever since. On and around the grounds of the Old Mint on Esplanade in the lower French Quarter, first weekend in August.

voyage.name: Southern Decadence
voyage.content: Each summer, big event for LGBTQ+ people and those who love and respect the LGBTQ+ community.

voyage.name: Tales of the Cocktail
voyage.content: An annual event each July in the Quarter and CBD with seminars, tastings, and other events, drawing in people from master bartenders to casual cocktail lovers. There's even a "jazz funeral" procession for the cocktail which top bartenders would most like to see buried (past "funerals" have included "sex on the beach" and the "appletini").

voyage.name: Bourbon Street
voyage.content: Some 8 blocks of Bourbon from Canal Street down are given over to catering to the hard drinking tourists. If getting drunk with other tourists is the goal of your vacation, this is the place for you. Even otherwise, this notorious strip of tourist traps is worth at least a quick look for its gaudy sleaziness. Bourbon has not only countless bars but also many fine restaurants featuring delicious local cuisine for peop

voyage.name: Royal Street
voyage.content: Strolling Royal Street by day is as essential a New Orleans experience as Bourbon Street by night. 1 block away in distance, a world in attitude. There are art galleries, upscale antique stores, landmark hotels and interesting specialty shops. Lots of temptations for those with money, but is also fun window shopping for those not spending a dime.

voyage.name: Jackson Square
voyage.content: The old town square, often live music is going on here, as well as street corner painters and tarot readers. Around the square are:.

voyage.name: Cabildo
voyage.price: $10 adults, $8 students/seniors/military, free for children 6 and under
voyage.content: Colonial city hall, now a museum; Louisiana Purchase agreements transferring the city from France to the USA were signed here.

voyage.name: Presbytere
voyage.price: $7 adults, $6 students/seniors/military, free for children 6 and under
voyage.content: Colonial church offices, now another museum, including exhibits on New Orleans Mardi Gras and the city's recovery from Hurricane Katrina.

voyage.name: St. Louis Cathedral
voyage.hours: The cathedral is open for self-guided tours daily from the end of morning mass until 4PM; see website for mass times
voyage.content: A symbol of New Orleans, this is the oldest Roman Catholic Cathedral in the United States and has a giant statue of the Virgin Mary with her arms extended gracing the middle of the courtyard.

voyage.name: Pontalba Buildings
voyage.content: 4-story brick apartment buildings have specialty shops, restaurants, and a tourist information office on the ground floors.

voyage.name: Moon Walk
voyage.content: A brick walking path along the Mississippi River across Decatur Street from Jackson Square. The curious name comes from its dedication to former New Orleans mayor Moon Landrieu.

voyage.name: Chartres Street
voyage.content: Parallels Bourbon and Royal Streets, one block closer to the river than Royal. While less famous with visitors, those who enjoy historic architecture will find the city's greatest concentration of preserved colonial era buildings along Chartres, along with early 19th century town-houses. Plus it passes through Jackson Square. A pleasant walk with local shops, cafes, restaurants, and bars scattered along the street.

voyage.name: Old French Market
voyage.address: bound by Ursulines Ave, N Peters St, Barracks St, and French Market Pl
voyage.content: While souvenirs for visitors have taken over a good bit of the space at this more than 250-year-old market, there are still vendors selling fresh produce as in days of old. On weekends a much larger number of vendors set up here, with handicrafts and flea market type goods.

voyage.name: Lower Decatur Street
voyage.content: Right around the corner from the historic US Mint, and the French Market. A French Quarter neighborhood with shops, dining, and entertainment. Late at night the bars really hop with local color.

voyage.name: New Orleans Jazz Park Visitor's Center & Headquarters
voyage.content: Often has live music, lectures, and gives music history related walking tours. Many events are free; those that aren't are a bargain.

voyage.name: Jean Lafitte National Park and Preserve
voyage.content: Headquarters for National Park that includes several historic sites in and near New Orleans. Has a small museum and visitor's center. Show up by 9AM to get a place on the informative free walking tour of the French Quarter.

voyage.name: Historic New Orleans Collection
voyage.content: Museum with changing exhibits of local history. Also has a research center nearby on Chartres Street.

voyage.name: Old U.S. Mint
voyage.price: $6 adults, $5 students/seniors/military, free for children 12 and under
voyage.content: Coins haven't been minted in New Orleans for decades, so the building is now a museum, with the minting process downstairs and the world's top exhibit on New Orleans jazz upstairs.

voyage.name: Old Ursuline Convent
voyage.price: $5 adults, $4 seniors, $3 students, free for children under 6
voyage.content: Completed in 1752, open for tours.

voyage.name: Pharmacy Museum
voyage.price: Guided Tours: Adult $15, Senior/Student/Military $10; Self-Guided: Adults $10, Senior/Student/Military $7. Children 6 and under: Free
voyage.hours: Guided Tours: Thu-Sat 10:00am - 11:00am. Self-Guided Tours: Tue & Wed 10:00am - 4:00pm; Thu-Sat 11:00am - 4:00pm
voyage.content: See and learn about medical practices of the mid 19th century. Calling ahead to verify hours is recommended. Reservations required for guided tours.

voyage.name: Cigar Factory New Orleans & Museum
voyage.content: History and tradition of one of New Orleans' oldest traditions -- cigar rolling! Watch the masters at work daily in the only operating cigar factory since the 1950s.

voyage.name: Musee Conti Wax Museum
voyage.content: Experience more than 300 years of history, legend and scandal with the 154 life-size figures displayed in historically accurate settings.

voyage.name: 1850 House
voyage.price: $3 adults, $2 students/seniors/military, free for children 12 and under

voyage.name: Beauregard-Keyes House
voyage.price: $10 adults, $9 students/seniors, $4 children 6-12, free for children under 6

voyage.name: Hermann-Grima House
voyage.price: $10 adults, $8 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members, free for children under 8. Joint admission with the Gallier House $18 adults, $15 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members
voyage.content: 1830s mansion.

voyage.name: Gallier House
voyage.price: $10 adults, $8 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members, free for children under 8. Joint admission with the Hermann-Grima House $18 adults, $15 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members
voyage.content: Home of famous local 19th-century architect.

voyage.name: Madame John's Legacy
voyage.content: 18th-century Creole home.

voyage.name: Carriage rides
voyage.content: Mule-drawn carriages have driven tourists around the Quarter since the gasoline rationing of the 1940s. Carriage drivers are licensed tour guides and give tourists a full blown tour consisting of a mix of history, architecture, restaurants & stories, though some drivers have been known to spin stories that are more colorful than factual. Available to tourists is a 30-minute tour of the French Quarter, hour tour of th

voyage.name: Street entertainers
voyage.content: Performing for tips from tourists, varying greatly in talent. The still mime-ers are a sight to see, they stand still alone or with a partner and when you give them a tip they will move very slowly in tandem, like a robot. There are excellent musicians who enjoy keeping up their chops out of doors. There are also hacks with little talent other than scamming money. Beware of the Got-yo-shoes-ers; these are scammers wh

voyage.name: Walking tours
voyage.content: Plentiful but often pricey. Most cost $10-20 per person, but there are a couple of good, free walking tours. Or you can simply walk and see all of the landmarks since most are labeled and you can go in and read about it yourself. Park rangers from the Jean Lafitte National Park (see above) offer a free walking tour of the French Quarter that is very informative. Space is very limited, and spots on the tour are only g

voyage.name: Aquarium of the Americas
voyage.content: The only aquarium in New Orleans. In the French Quarter. Features an IMAX theatre. 10AM-5PM daily.

voyage.name: Audubon Insectarium
voyage.content: In the historic Old Customs House Building. The Audubon Institute, which also runs the nearby Aquarium and the Zoo up in the Audubon District, opened the Insectarium in 2008. 10a-5p daily.

voyage.name: Fritzels
voyage.content: Good house bands in the evenings, and is often a venue for out-of-town and international musicians versed in the New Orleans style.

voyage.name: Maison Bourbon
voyage.content: Sometimes has decent bands (though as often doesn't), as many good local Dixieland players lacking a better gig for the moment often wind up here. As the doors are open to the street, you can listen a bit from outside, judge for yourself whether they have a band you'd enjoy, and walk on by or go on in as appropriate.

voyage.name: New Orleans Jazz Park
voyage.price: Free, some park programs have a fee
voyage.content: Actually in "Dutch Alley", the French Market pedestrian alley on the river side of Decatur between Dumaine and St. Philip Streets. Often has free live music weekend afternoons and sometimes other times.

voyage.name: Palm Court Jazz Cafe
voyage.content: Those who prefer their old style New Orleans jazz in a somewhat more upscale atmosphere where dinner and drinks are served should be sure to visit this place in the lower Quarter. Some of the same musicians who play Preservation Hall play here on other nights, along with other top local classic style jazz greats. The owner's husband runs the Jazzology record company, featuring the world's largest independent label ca

voyage.name: Preservation Hall
voyage.price: 45-minute set: front row $50, seated $40, standing room $25 for advance online purchase seats (cash purchase at the door is no longer available)
voyage.content: Established in 1961 to preserve Traditional New Orleans jazz. Talk about atmosphere! Listen to real jazz and nothing else (no booze, no bathrooms). You'll have to stand in line, and most people will stand through the set (accommodations will be made for those who can't stand that long; call +1 504-522-2841, or email info@preservationhall.com in advance). Sets each night from 5PM, Sa and Su from 2:30PM. Arrive at leas

voyage.name: Santa's Quarters
voyage.content: Christmas decorations. They have thousands of ornaments including New Orleans and Mardi Gras themed.

voyage.name: Latin's Hand
voyage.content: Explore the variety of Latin American, handmade goods, from hats to hammocks to all kinds of bags.

voyage.name: Cella's Boutique
voyage.content: Specializes in selling stylish, comfortable cotton and linen clothing, but also sells handmade accessories and shoes.

voyage.name: Arcadian Books & Art Prints
voyage.content: With stacks of books filling every available surface, this is a sight to be seen (and maybe some photos posted so your friends will believe you when you get home and try to describe it to them). This is a good choice if you're love browsing through used books and don't mind packed-full shelves and partially blocked aisles in your search for a possibly overlooked treasure. Some non-English books. Staff is helpful and

voyage.name: Acme Oyster House
voyage.content: No ambiance, but good oysters and other southern delights. Be ready to wait in line. Great food, Great price. 1/2 dozen chargrilled oysters for $9.99 simply can't be beat, especially since Louisiana oysters are far superior in size to those from anyplace else. For an entertaining and social experience, sit at the bar, where you can talk to the oyster shuckers about the celebrities and pro athletes who have visited in

voyage.name: Bennachin
voyage.content: African food. Good lunch specials. Many vegetarian and vegan options.

voyage.name: Cafe Envie
voyage.content: Sandwiches, salads, omelets, quiches. Wireless internet access.

voyage.name: Central Grocery
voyage.content: Old Italian-American grocery sandwich shop, famous for their enormous muffuletta sandwiches originated by this family in 1910. One is enough to feed four hungry people! Order 1/2 to start for 2 people!

voyage.name: Clover Grill
voyage.content: Good eggs, burgers, and such. Heavily (though not exclusively) gay clientele. They cook your burger under a hubcap!

voyage.name: Coop's Place
voyage.content: You can get good Cajun food at a really good price here. Locals favorite. Best fried chicken in the city! Patrons must be 21 or older to enter due to the presence of video poker machines.

voyage.name: Felix's Restaurant & Oyster Bar
voyage.content: The Acme's traditional competition and usually a shorter wait, too. A very good oyster bar with other traditional Cajun fare.

voyage.name: Jimani
voyage.content: When you want a great roast beef sandwich at 2AM.

voyage.name: Johnny's Po-Boys
voyage.content: Lunch counter with some eat-in tables; one of the largest po-boy menus around. Excellent breakfast biscuit sandwich!

voyage.name: Mona Lisa's
voyage.content: Italian and pizza.

voyage.name: Port of Call
voyage.content: Awesome, huge burgers and loaded baked potatoes. Potent drinks, parrot-head juke box. Lil slice of paradise.

voyage.name: Yo Mama's Bar and Grill
voyage.content: Limited but high quality grill menu, including 14 types of burgers.

voyage.name: Rampart Treehouse
voyage.content: Pizza Slice Bar that serves a rich pizza menu, art, cocktails, and beer. Our space is covered from floor to ceiling in artwork that is from artists from around the globe.

voyage.name: Cafe du Monde
voyage.content: Serves coffee and beignets. The cafe has been a local landmark since the 19th century and is across the street from St Ann St, which faces Jackson Square. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the cafe was open 24 hours daily. It often attracted long lines and crowds of locals and tourists during both the day and night. After a temporary shutdown at the beginning of the pandemic, the cafe has since reopened.

voyage.name: CC's Coffee House
voyage.content: The lower French Quarter branch of a small local chain. Great iced coffee drinks for hot days.

voyage.name: Croissant d'Or
voyage.hours: Mon, Wed-Fri 7AM-1PM; Sat & Sun 7AM-3PM; Closed Tue
voyage.content: French pastries and light breakfasts & lunch.

voyage.name: Bayona
voyage.content: Incredible French/Euro/NOLA food by esteemed chef, Susan Spicer. Fabulous wine selections. Many locals' favorite. Must RSVP.

voyage.name: French Market Restaurant and Bar
voyage.content: Serves boiled crawfish and other down-home delicacies. Happy hour M-F 3-5PM with raw oysters $.50 each. Has downstairs restaurant and balcony seating upstairs.

voyage.name: El Gato Negro
voyage.content: A local favorite for Mexican. Breakfast available on the weekends.

voyage.name: Green Goddess
voyage.content: Small restaurant tucked away on a side street serving creative dishes. Opened in 2009 and quickly became a favorite with local foodies. A few years later it's certainly been "discovered"; try to go there sometime other than the busiest days and not during the busiest dinner hours to avoid long waits for a table.

voyage.name: Gumbo Shop
voyage.content: An institution for gumbos and similar traditional Louisiana dishes.

voyage.name: Italian Barrel
voyage.content: Northern Italian cuisine with an Italian-focused wine list. The outdoor tables are across from the New Orleans Jazz Museum’s outdoor stage, and Frenchmen Street’s live-music venues are nearby. Reservations are recommended during peak dinner hours.

voyage.name: Louisiana Pizza Kitchen
voyage.content: Upscale pizzeria in the French Market.

voyage.name: Mr. B's Bistro
voyage.content: Storied, elegant restaurant whose signature dish is the (non-grilled) BBQ shrimp.

voyage.name: Remoulade
voyage.content: A casual spin-off of Arnaud's where you can try their famous Caesar salad dressing and the eponymous remoulade without wearing a jacket and tie. Same shrimp remoulade and gumbo as the main restaurant for a lower price.

voyage.name: Sylvain
voyage.content: Opened in 2010; quality food and drink in a beautiful Spanish Colonial era building.

voyage.name: Tujague's
voyage.content: Pronounced "two jacks"; despite the weird spelling, it's been here since 1856 so they must be doing something right. The locals swear by it.

voyage.name: Antoine's
voyage.content: Antoine's lays claim to being the oldest same family owned restaurant in the country. Opening in 1840, this French Creole restaurant is where Oysters Rockefeller was invented in the 1890s -- and the only restaurant where the original authentic Oysters Rockefeller can be eaten, as the recipe is a closely guarded secret. Your waiter is your guide here; treat them well and ask their recommendations. Before dining, ask y

voyage.name: Arnaud's
voyage.content: Another of the great old French Quarter classics.

voyage.name: Brennan's
voyage.content: One of the famous local traditions; fine Creole cuisine, known for their gourmet breakfasts. Ask to sit in the courtyard, on the balcony, or in one of the upstairs rooms. Be sure to try the Bananas Foster, which was invented here. Great for upscale New Orleans breakfast.

voyage.name: Court of Two Sisters
voyage.content: A place for daily brunch (with a live jazz combo) and post-night out hangover cures; beautiful courtyard.

voyage.name: Galatoire's
voyage.content: Classic Creole on Bourbon Street. Despite being in the tourist strip of Bourbon Street, locals do eat here. For the true experience, wait in line for the downstairs dining room (reservations can be made for the upstairs room, but locals don't eat there), and refuse the menu when you're seated. Let your waiter know your tastes and let him feed you.

voyage.name: NOLA
voyage.content: Very good, run by chef Emeril Lagasse, not quite as pricey as his namesake restaurant in the Central Business District, and not as severe a dress code.

voyage.name: Aunt Tiki's
voyage.content: Punk version of a tiki bar on Lower Decatur.

voyage.name: The Bombay Club
voyage.content: High-end cocktails with a dress code.

voyage.name: Cafe Lafitte in Exile
voyage.content: Claims to be the USA's oldest gay bar ("in exile" since the original Lafitte's (see below) went straight back in the Eisenhower Administration). Everyone welcome.

voyage.name: Carousel Bar
voyage.content: Renowned for generations for the slowly rotating "Carousel" section; also has non-rotating seating.

voyage.name: Crescent City Brewhouse
voyage.content: Microbrewery, also serves food.

voyage.name: The Dungeon
voyage.content: Two dark gothic bars (having split up some ten years ago) open at midnight. The "Original Dungeon" has a bit more cooler atmosphere, but fewer patrons, since it's a little harder to find--down an alley next to "Front of the Dungeon." The Front of the Dungeon's bathroom is a hoot, hidden behind a secret door in the bookcases, and with a toilet so bad as to be borderline unapproachable.

voyage.name: Fritzels
voyage.content: Best known as a trad jazz venue, but also has a bar with good draft German beer even when there isn't live music.

voyage.name: Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop
voyage.content: Piano bar towards the end of the touristy part of Bourbon Street, lit entirely by candlelight. Supposedly once the in-town headquarters of pirate & smuggler Jean Lafitte, many colorful stories are told about this location. They pour great Hurricanes.

voyage.name: Molly's at the Market
voyage.content: A great Irish/Quarterpunk bar, long a favorite of bohemian locals.

voyage.name: Molly's On Toulouse
voyage.content: A local Irish pub with a pool table & the best juke box in the French Quarter. Irish Car Bombs are $5.50! Great selection of Irish Whiskeys.

voyage.name: Napoleon House
voyage.content: The place to go if you like the thought of good drinks in a more than 200-year-old building whose owners are proud that the interior hasn't been repainted since World War I, with classical music playing over the sound system. Napoleon never made it here, as he died before the local plan to rescue him from exile and start his empire afresh in Louisiana could be carried out. Napoleon House also serves good sandwiches a

voyage.name: Oz
voyage.content: Loud hip gay disco.

voyage.name: Parade
voyage.content: New Orleans' largest gay nightclub since 1974.

voyage.name: Pat O'Brien's
voyage.content: Famous for strong Hurricanes, Mint Juleps, TNTs, Purple People Eaters; popular tourist hangout for a reason. Has been trendy for generations. Has an impressive fire/water fountain and patio.

voyage.name: Tropical Isle
voyage.content: Home of the Hand Grenade, "New Orleans's Most Powerful Drink", is a staple of Bourbon Street decadence. Definitely a must-try.

voyage.name: Brieux Carre
voyage.content: Small craft brewery located off of Frenchman St. Has a good selection with a primary focus on sours and stouts. Good pilsners.

voyage.name: Andrew Jackson Hotel
voyage.content: One of the oldest hotels in the French Quarter.

voyage.name: Crowne Plaza New Orleans French Quarter
Bienville House
voyage.content: Lovely courtyard, pool and balconies

voyage.name: Bourbon Orleans
voyage.content: Built in 1817.

voyage.name: La Galerie Hotel French Quarter
voyage.content: This 80-year-old inn offers a complimentary continental breakfast in its elegant lobby.

voyage.name: French Market Inn
voyage.content: Great location with reasonable rates, it's known for its courtyard atmosphere.

voyage.name: Courtyard New Orleans French Quarter/Iberville
voyage.content: Caters to business, leisure, family, and is also gay/lesbian friendly. Spacious suites with huge bed, kitchen, large bathroom, living room with fold out, and 2 TVs. Valet parking, free bell-hop, lots of amenities, and free breakfast. They also feature fantastic massages at their spa.

voyage.name: Four Points by Sheraton French Quarter
voyage.content: A beautiful historic hotel on the site of the old French Opera House. Notable for its balconies overlooking Bourbon and Toulouse Streets and a beautiful courtyard with pool.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn Chateau LeMoyne
voyage.content: An historic hotel occupying what were four 19th-century townhomes.

voyage.name: Lafitte Guest House
voyage.content: A boutique hotel in the residential area of Bourbon Street. Visitors will enjoy the sights and sounds of Bourbon Street as well as a retreat into their own personal French Quarter home.

voyage.name: Hotel Monteleone
voyage.content: In an elegant early-20th century skyscraper (the only one within the confines of the Quarter itself, just constructed just before large new constructions were prohibited here) has long been one of the top upscale Quarter hotels. The hotel includes a rooftop heated pool with views of the skyline and an award-winning restaurant, the Hunt Room Grill.

voyage.name: Omni Royal Orleans
voyage.content: The Omni Royal Orleans has been a recipient of the AAA four-diamond award for the past 27 years.

voyage.name: Royal Barracks Guest House
voyage.content: Every room features a queen-sized bed, private bath and fireplace, and private entrance to the courtyard.

voyage.name: Hotel Mazarin
voyage.content: Luxurious furnishings, with a beautiful courtyard.

voyage.name: Hotel St. Pierre
voyage.content: Embodies the architecture and ambiance of the 18th-century French Quarter.

voyage.name: Ursuline Guest House
voyage.content: 13 guest rooms, each with private bath, ceiling fan, air conditioning/heating, cable television and wireless Internet access.

voyage.name: Maison Dupuy
voyage.content: This hotel has a beautiful courtyard with a real New Orleans atmosphere; renovated historic homes surround what is now the courtyard with a fountain and pool.

voyage.name: Hotel Royal
voyage.content: On the finest shopping street in the French Quarter, this hotel has a European feeling complemented by authentic laced iron balconies, high ceilings with fans, and enclosed courtyards with fountains.

voyage.name: French Quarter Landmark Hotel
voyage.content: Within walking distance of the hotel, explore the historic, artistic and eclectic charms around you.

voyage.name: Hotel Le Marais
voyage.content: A heated saltwater courtyard pool and breakfast area.

voyage.name: Place D'Armes
voyage.content: Beautiful historic hotel in the quarter. They have interior rooms (no windows) that are a great bargain to stay in an incredible space.

voyage.name: Hotel Maison de Ville
voyage.content: One of the most historic hotels in the Quarter, everyone from Tennessee Williams to Audobon has spent time there.

voyage.name: W New Orleans French Quarter
voyage.content: Boutique hotel.

voyage.name: City House Hostel
voyage.content: Free wireless internet, 24 hour reception. 14 night maximum stay.

voyage.name: IHSP French Quarter House
voyage.content: Free wireless internet, free breakfast, 24 hour reception. Dorm rooms only open to students and foreign travelers, and there is a 7 night maximum stay.

voyage.name: French Quarter Mansion
voyage.content: Gay-friendly bed and breakfast in the center of the Quarter.

voyage.name: Audubon Aquarium of the Americas
voyage.content: A fine aquarium at the foot of Canal Street. Take advantage of the combination ticket, which enables access to the Aquarium, the adjoining Entergy IMAX Theatre, and the Audubon Zoo which is uptown (shuttle provided).

voyage.name: Entergy IMAX Theatre
voyage.content: Part of the Audubon Aquarium.

voyage.name: Audubon Insectarium
voyage.content: An attraction opened in 2008 in the historic old Custom House Building on Canal Street. As it's in a Federal building, you'll pass through a metal detector.

voyage.name: Confederate Museum
voyage.content: Displays from the American Civil War.

voyage.name: Lafayette Square
voyage.address: bound by St. Charles Ave, Camp St, N Maestri St, and S Maestri St
voyage.content: The center of what was the "Old American Quarter" in the early 19th century, with the city's neo-classical city hall and a belle epoch courthouse.

voyage.name: Mardi Gras World
voyage.content: The colorful floats for many of the parades of New Orleans Mardi Gras are made here. Experience a taste of Mardi Gras any time of year.

voyage.name: Caesars Superdome
voyage.content: It was built as the Louisiana Superdome, and is home of the NFL's New Orleans Saints. When no games or events are scheduled, you can take tours.

voyage.name: Smoothie King Center
voyage.content: Located beside the Superdome, the Smoothie King Center (formerly New Orleans Arena) hosts smaller shows & sporting events. Most notably home to the NBA's New Orleans Pelicans.

voyage.name: Morial Convention Center
voyage.content: The first part of the city's large convention center complex was built during the 1984 World's Fair and is named after a former mayor.

voyage.name: National World War II Museum
voyage.content: Formerly the "D-Day Museum". Exhibits on the United States in World War II on the battlefronts and the home front. It has a restaurant, the "Victory Theater" presenting multi-media historical presentation, and the "Stage Door Canteen" featuring live music shows in the style of World War II-era USO shows.

voyage.name: Caesars New Orleans
voyage.content: The state's only land-based casino (there are riverboat gambling venues in the suburbs).

voyage.name: Howlin' Wolf
voyage.content: They host a good variety of local and visiting acts; definitely get a hold of their schedule in The Gambit, a weekly paper. (If you visited here before Katrina, they are now a block up the street from their former location.)

voyage.name: Mulate's
voyage.content: At Convention Center Boulevard. Cajun music.

voyage.name: Orpheum Theatre
voyage.content: Home of the Louisiana Philharmonic Orchestra.

voyage.name: Saenger Theater
voyage.content: At Canal Street. The most gorgeous of the city's beautiful old picture palace theaters.

voyage.name: Le Salon
voyage.content: Swanky hotel bar often has good jazz pianists, vocalists, and small combos.

voyage.name: Meyer the Hatter
voyage.content: Has been selling a wide selection of men's hats here since 1894.

voyage.name: Riverwalk
voyage.content: On a pier along the Mississippi Riverfront and connected to the New Orleans Hilton. In addition to a variety of shops, hosts a fine view of the Mississippi River.

voyage.name: Cafe Du Monde
voyage.content: Sells chicory-flavored coffee with New Orleans beignets.

voyage.name: City Greens
voyage.content: Soups, salad, wraps; breakfast & lunch.

voyage.name: La Boca
voyage.content: Argentine steak house.

voyage.name: Merchant
voyage.content: Crepes, quiches, sandwiches, salads.

voyage.name: Mulate's
voyage.content: At Convention Center Boulevard. The other well known Cajun place.

voyage.name: Emeril's
voyage.content: In the Warehouse District.

voyage.name: Grill Room at Windsor Court Hotel
voyage.content: Contender for best restaurant, but very expensive; in the CBD just down from the Casino. They also serve a fine high-tea.

voyage.name: Palace Cafe
voyage.content: French Creole, noted for the seafood and duck dishes, and the luscious white chocolate bread pudding.

voyage.name: Restaurant August
voyage.content: Renowned chef John Besh's signature restaurant featuring Contemporary French with a focus on local ingredients. Menu balances seafood, fowl and meat. Try either the 5 course tasting or the John Besh "Degustation" menu which changes nightly.

voyage.name: Gordon Biersch
voyage.content: Handcrafted beer brewery and restaurant.

voyage.name: Lucy's Retired Surfer Bar
voyage.content: Relaxed. All-you-can-eat crawfish party Sunday evenings.

voyage.name: Sazerac Bar
voyage.content: In the Roosevelt Hotel. Sip signature drinks like the original Sazerac cocktail or the Ramos gin fiz.

voyage.name: Whiskey Blue
voyage.content: Swank upscale bar

voyage.name: Hostelling International
voyage.content: This hostel offers both shared dorms and ensuite private rooms. Bathrooms for dorm guests are in the hallway, but they are all single-use. Dorms also have security lockers. Free breakfast and free wireless internet available.

voyage.name: Les Carillons
voyage.content: Towards the upper end of the CBD, close to the Julia Street art galleries.

voyage.name: Embassy Suites New Orleans - Convention Center
Hilton New Orleans Riverside
voyage.content: 3-star Hilton on the banks of the Mississippi River, in storied New Orleans, Louisiana adjacent to the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center and only three blocks from the French Quarter.

voyage.name: Courtyard New Orleans Downtown/Convention Center
voyage.content: Two blocks from Morial Convention Center.

voyage.name: Hyatt Place New Orleans Convention Center
voyage.content: Across the street from the New Orleans Convention Center. It offers upscale lodging.

voyage.name: Hyatt Regency New Orleans
voyage.content: Near the Superdome and City Hall.

voyage.name: InterContinental New Orleans
voyage.content: Luxury hotel on the St. Charles Mardi Gras parade route.

voyage.name: International House Hotel
voyage.content: Boutique hotel 2 blocks from the French Quarter.

voyage.name: Le Pavillon
voyage.content: One of the fanciest hotels in the city with the exception of the Ritz Carlton and Windsor Court. Elegant French and Old South stylings in the lobby. Featuring a Sunday "Jazz Brunch" with live music as well as a rooftop jacuzzi.

voyage.name: Loft 523
voyage.content: Boutique hotel 2 blocks from the French Quarter.

voyage.name: Ritz-Carlton
voyage.content: Top notch hotel in what had been the Maison Blanche Department Store building. It's the Windsor Court's rival for finest in town.

voyage.name: The Roosevelt
voyage.content: One of the city's grand old hotels; reopened in 2009 after a $145-million restoration modernized the rooms, returned the lobby to its historic glory, and reopened the famous Sazerac Bar and the Blue Room dinner & music venue. The lobby is worth a look even if you're not staying here.

voyage.name: The Whitney
voyage.content: A New Orleans hotel registered as a historic landmark.

voyage.name: Windsor Court Hotel
voyage.content: One of the finer hotels in town, If you want the tops and are willing to pay top dollar for it, this is the place.

voyage.name: Cafe Istanbul
voyage.content: Named after a legendary Frenchmen Street venue of a generation ago, the new Cafe Istanbul is theater space with a bar in the New Orleans Healing Center, a renovated old warehouse building now a community center. Live theater, music, dance, film, and other performances.

voyage.name: Louisiana Music Factory
voyage.content: Specializes in local music, with a wide selection new and used CDs, plus vintage vinyl upstairs. Local musicians often play free sets here for promotion when they come out with a new record. The staff here usually know their stuff and can make good recommendations.

voyage.name: Scott Edwards Photography Studio & Gallery
voyage.content: A gallery specializing in regional and New Orleans based Photography.

voyage.name: Island of Salvation Botanica
voyage.content: A real voodoo supply store. Moved from their old ramshackle building in the Bywater into the new "Healing Center" building in 2011.

voyage.name: 13 Monaghan
voyage.content: An Irish themed bar and grill, squeezed into an odd warehouse space. Good Irish beers and late-night grub, including Huevos Rancheros and pulled pork sandwich. Vegan options available.

voyage.name: Cafe Rose Nicaud
voyage.content: Coffees, teas, and fresh deli sandwiches, quiches.

voyage.name: Cake Cafe
voyage.content: Great bakery with sandwiches.

voyage.name: Flora Gallery and Coffee Shop
voyage.content: Ultra-funky coffeehouse with light fare, as well as poetry readings, board games, and the like.

voyage.name: Mona's
voyage.content: Middle Eastern cuisine, with excellent shwarmas, and an extensive vegetarian selection. Other locations around the city.

voyage.name: Schiro's Community Cafe & Bar
voyage.content: Great food, reasonably priced. Great vegan/vegetarian selections, even for breakfast. Small community market attached.

voyage.name: WhoDat Coffee
voyage.alt: formerly Hallowed Grounds, formerly Marigny Perks
voyage.content: Friendly coffee shop with free wireless internet and easy parking. Gourmet coffee and tea, soup, salad, sandwich and pastry selection, reasonably priced.

voyage.name: Breakaway's R & B
voyage.content: Your Favorite Creole Cookhouse in The Marigny.New Orleans Unofficial Rock & Roll Hall of FameFrom the Chef of Green Goddess. The name is inspired by Irma Thomas’ song “Breakaway.” The R&B means restaurant and bar more than rhythm and blues, but the Artigues liked the idea of a reference to local music to help set the tone for their neighborhood place.

voyage.name: Alois J. Binder Bakery
voyage.content: Breads and pastries to go.

voyage.name: The Orange Couch
voyage.content: Coffee house with light snacks, ice cream, and WiFi.

voyage.name: Adolfo's
voyage.content: Cozy, slightly quirky yet charming Italian. Let the waiters guide you to the nightly specials.

voyage.name: Feelings Cafe
voyage.content: The way the French Quarter used to be 50 years ago. Great piano bar, balcony overlooking nice courtyard. Definitely a locals place and great value, but not for the homophobic.

voyage.name: Marigny Brasserie
voyage.content: Good menu, and a popular wine and martini bar.

voyage.name: Praline Connection
voyage.content: Much more than pralines (a sweet pecan candy), good Creole soul food at a reasonable price.

voyage.name: Sukho Thai
voyage.content: Authentic Thai food in a neighborhood cafe.

voyage.name: Wasabi
voyage.content: Excellent sushi and Japanese cuisine. Good selection of sakes.

voyage.name: Apple Barrel
voyage.content: Sometimes has live music too. Local characters, low prices, no attitude.

voyage.name: AllWays
voyage.content: Lounge in the front, small theater in the back. The hub of fringe theater, plays, bands, and variety shows often. Very friendly and comfortable for all.

voyage.name: d.b.a.
voyage.content: New York style bar on Frenchmen, if you need a bit of sophistication when you drink. Great selection of beers, and frequent live music.

voyage.name: Dragon's Den
voyage.content: A charmingly dilapidated, well-hidden club (go down the building's side alley, then up the stairs to your left), with a balcony on Esplanade and an opium-den feel inside. Live music, occasional poetry slams, serves food.

voyage.name: Friendly Bar
voyage.content: Gay neighborhood bar where locals gather to hang out in a no-pressure atmosphere.

voyage.name: Iggy's
voyage.content: Neighborhood bar with a lot of neighborhood characters; very friendly for all. Frequently serves food.

voyage.name: The John
voyage.content: Relaxed neighborhood hangout with rockabilly, country, and punk on the jukebox. Named for the gold-painted toilet seats that serve as stools at the tables. With inexpensive stiff drinks served up in Mason jars, this spot for locals offers one of the best deals on Frenchmen St.

voyage.name: Mimi's in the Marigny
voyage.content: The toniest bar in the Marigny (but hardly pretentious), with billiards, Galaga, occasional live music, and tapas served from the restaurant upstairs. Good selection of beers and specialty drinks. Hip Hop and Funk DJs Friday and Saturday nights. Lots of singles on the weekends.

voyage.name: Phoenix
voyage.content: Gay neighborhood bar by day, catering to the leather crowd at night. Also the official United Cab stand for catching rides back into the French Quarter.

voyage.name: R-Bar
voyage.content: Hip but laid-back hangout that's comfortable by day and happening at night; great jukebox.

voyage.name: Blue Nile
voyage.content: A staple of the Frenchmen Street set of music venues, Blue Nile serves up funk, blues, jazz, and New Orleans-style brass bands. A plus is the big dance floor. Unlike most places in Marigny, though, it often charges a cover, so be sure to sample the music from outside before making the decision to go in.

voyage.name: Buffa's Lounge
voyage.content: Small bar room in the front; the big room in the back (also accessible from the side door on Burgundy Street) hosts live music and other events, including a popular jazz brunch on Sundays.

voyage.name: Checkpoint Charlies
voyage.content: This bar has bands, pool tables and laundry facilities if your clothes need awashin'. Local rock and jump bands.

voyage.name: The Maison
voyage.content: The place to go for dinner + jazz (pretty energetic jazz), with the largest dining room on the street, and three stages for music.

voyage.name: Snug Harbor
voyage.content: Perhaps the city's foremost modern jazz venue.

voyage.name: The Spotted Cat Music Club
voyage.content: Cozy bar with good hot jazz.

voyage.name: Aaron Ingram Haus
voyage.content: One and two bedroom suites six blocks from Bourbon Street.

voyage.name: Auld Sweet Olive Bed and Breakfast
voyage.content: Historic home with six rooms, each with private bath. Hand painted wall treatments, attractive gardens.

voyage.name: B&W Courtyards
voyage.content: Three 19th century buildings connected by lush courtyards. Private baths. Architectural award winner.

voyage.name: 1870 Banana Courtyard B&B
voyage.content: In 1800s former elite bordello. B&B now. Balcony rooms with a view or budget rooms, each w/different theme. Lagniappe: free soft drinks, bottled water, generous continental breakfast. Tropical courtyard with hammock, verandah with porch swing. Wi-Fi. New fangled stuff, ensuite like: private bathrooms, cable TV, phone, heat and A/C. Gated parking lot.

voyage.name: The Burgundy Bed and Breakfast
voyage.content: Gay owned and operated, affordable rates.

voyage.name: Chez Nous Guest House
voyage.content: One and two bedroom private suites.

voyage.name: The Claiborne Mansion
voyage.content: An outstanding 19th century mansion and a wonderful hostess, Cleo. .

voyage.name: Creole Inn
voyage.content: A cozy and affordable B&B.

voyage.name: Crescent City Guest House
voyage.content: 4 Guest rooms each with private bathrooms. All taxes, maid service and continental breakfast included. Free off-street parking and WiFi.

voyage.name: Elysian Fields Inn
voyage.content: Hosts, Leigh and Jim are very knowledgeable of the NOLA music scene. Has secure covered parking.

voyage.name: La Dauphine, Residence des Artistes
voyage.content: A Bohemian, laid-back, unpretentious, 2 room 1896 guest house for the budget-minded traveler- with a 3-night minimum; private baths, free Internet. Advance reservations required. Ray & Kim are the warm and friendly hosts.

voyage.name: La Maison Marigny Bed and Breakfast
voyage.content: One of Travel & Leisure Magazine's TOP TEN B&Bs.

voyage.name: Maison DuBois Bed and Breakfast
voyage.content: Bed and breakfast.

voyage.name: Marigny Manor House
voyage.content: 1840s Grand Greek Revival home.

voyage.name: Old Town Inn
voyage.content: Cool historic inn, three separate buildings, dating from the 1800s.

voyage.name: Pierre Coulon Guest House
voyage.content: Comfortable small apartment.

voyage.name: River House
voyage.content: A lovingly-restored antebellum mansion with three unique apartments, each like no other.

voyage.name: Royal Street Inn B&B
voyage.content: "B&B" here may stand for "Bed and Beverage", as this is upstairs from the R-Bar.

voyage.name: Suite Jazz
voyage.content: Circa 1861, the building has typical high ceilings, chandeliers, hardwood floors, Cable TV, WIFI Internet Access, Central Air, a fully stocked kitchen and more! A queen sleigh bed, travertine tiled shower & original artwork by fabulous artists. Windows have added sound protection. Sylvia is one of New Orleans' best ambassadors and a great concierge/hostess/tour guide.

voyage.name: Sunburst Inn
voyage.content: Historic Victorian house with one and two bedroom suites with private bath. A short walk to French Quarter. Suites has lots of nice amenities, located in quite charming neighborhood.

voyage.name: Lions Inn Bed and Breakfast
voyage.content: Features ten non-smoking guest rooms. Most have private baths while some share a bath. All have twin, king, and queen-sized beds. Among its most appealing features is a garden with swimming pool and Jacuzzi hot tub.

voyage.name: River House New Orleans
voyage.content: Three-story antebellum guest house with separate apartments on each floor. Amenities include complementary Wi-Fi and a swimming pool. Rates are lower during the summer (June 1-August 31) and higher during special events (Mardi Gras, French Quarter Fest, New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, Halloween, and New Years Eve). All payments must go through Airbnb or VRBO. A 2-night minimum stay is required.

voyage.name: St Claude Arts District/SCAD
voyage.content: New Orleans newest and hottest arts district that's not your usual tourist-centric arts destination. A true "only in New Orleans" experience. Check website for current exhibits, times, and addresses.

voyage.name: The Great War Memorial
voyage.content: The first of it kind erected at the end of WWI, this monument pays tribute the fallen residents of the 9th Ward.

voyage.name: Vaughan's Lounge
voyage.content: Bywater's most famous music venue. Thursday nights when righteous-trumpter/bandleader Kermit Ruffins is in town, he and his BBQ swingers play here; Thursday with Kermit as Vaughan's is a New Orleans favorite. 8:30 PM they say; don't expect shows to start at their clock time in New Orleans, but now that Kermit is a family man, things here tend to start a bit more punctually than they did years ago. Expect crowds and g

voyage.name: Sankofa Marketplace
voyage.content: Weekly market with farm fresh produce, prepared food, crafts. The second Saturday of each month also has live music and other special events; sometimes music other Saturdays as well.

voyage.name: The Spellcaster Lodge
voyage.content: Home of the Amazing Mr. Quintron, Miss Pussycat, and the Drum Buddy workshops. Only open a handful of nights in the year, but this is home to some wild bohemian parties and performances, and, as a visitor, you'll really blow the locals' minds for simply knowing of the place. Stop in if you get a chance.

voyage.name: Alombrados Oasis
voyage.content: This temple of the Ordo Templi Orientis hosts performances of The Gnostic Mass, conducts initiatory ceremonies, seasonal mystery plays, frequent classes on Thelema, Magick, Yoga, Gnosticism, QBL, Hermetic and Rosicrucian Science, and intensive training programs of Scientific Illuminism. The Oasis also hosts occasional art shows featuring local artists. Contact by phone to attend events. thumb|300px| The Alombrados Oa

voyage.name: Chazfest
voyage.content: Annual one day music festival held the first Wednesday in April, between the Jazz Fest weekends. (The name is a pun on "Jazz Fest" and popular local bandleader "Washboard Chaz".) 10 hours of great local music on 2 outdoor stages.

voyage.name: Dr Bob's Art Gallery
voyage.hours: Officially open by appointment only, but if you're passing by and see the gates open with the
voyage.content: A small gallery run by local self-taught folk artist, (you'll see examples of his work at local bars, cafes, and restaurants all over town) with eccentric artwork for sale that will immediately conjure New Orleans and the nearby Cajun Country.

voyage.name: Country Club
voyage.content: Upscale and stylish American cuisine at great prices, with dining in a beautiful old dining room or on the veranda overlooking the pool. It's a great brunch place. Gay and straight friendly private club and pool in rear, where you can sip cocktails in the jacuzzi into the night (note that it becomes clothing optional).

voyage.name: Elizabeth's
voyage.content: This is a real local favorite, particularly for breakfast/brunch. Creole and southern food dominates the menu, which combines with friendly service and a cute setting to make for a nice meal any time of day, though. If you have a sweet tooth, don't skip the praline bacon!

voyage.name: Frady's
voyage.content: This is the sort of place you would only know about if you get a local recommendation—it won't be in your guidebook. For the most part, this is simply a corner store, but the po' boys, particularly the oyster po' boy, are some of the best you'll ever eat. The old-timey Bywater feel to the place is an added plus.

voyage.name: Jack Dempsey's
voyage.content: This is about as divey and old-school New Orleans as a seafood restaurant can possibly be—you can't be much further from the four star contemporary American dining in Uptown and the Quarter. It's so dark inside, you'll hardly be able to see your big plate of heavily fried seafood and delicious mac 'n cheese (the seafood gumbo and po' boys are decent too).

voyage.name: The Joint
voyage.content: Excellent down home barbecue with a casual, wooden picnic table-style dining room. If you are trying to decide between Bywater BBQ and the Joint, they are both great; it's a matter of preference between the Joint's dryer style and Bywater BBQ's more wet slabs. Aim first for the ribs and the pulled pork, but really everything is great here.

voyage.name: Markey's Bar
voyage.content: Great pub food in what can only be described as a standard, classic neighborhood bar (with a few microbrews on tap). Big juicy burgers, fresh salads, and the best wings in the neighborhood. Daily specials and crawfish on Fridays (in season).

voyage.name: Satsuma's Cafe
voyage.content: A rather hip spot to get your yuppie-ish fix of "fair trade" espresso, fresh juices, quiches, salads, sandwiches, etc. The popularity means long waits on weekends, but the high quality does actually merit the wait.

voyage.name: Suis Generis
voyage.content: Eclectic innovative cuisine in matching decor. Fresh, tasty, and distinctive.

voyage.name: Bacchanal
voyage.content: Wine shop, offers wine by the glass—and irregularly has visiting chefs prepare gourmet treats. Now offers lunch too.

voyage.name: BJ's Lounge
voyage.content: Friendly neighborhood dive with a colorful cast of characters. Beer and booze bar-you're not gonna get an apple martini here. Cookoffs and potlucks are fairly frequent, occasional live music. If you are at Vaughan's Lounge, hop on in and get a bit stronger dose of Bywater.

voyage.name: Saturn Bar
voyage.content: This is a strange old bohemian dive with some of the city's funkiest and most bizarre decor-soaked in neon and covered in old-school sci-fi posters (sadly, the old jukebox that only played Frank Sinatra's Witchcraft regardless of what you picked is defunct). Drink cheap beer, whiskey, or Southern Comfort. Don't expect them to know how to make fancy-pants mixed drinks. Occasional live music. Rumored to be the favorite

voyage.name: Vaughan's Lounge
voyage.content: Famous as a music venue, but when it isn't hopping with live music a nice place to get a drink and a bit to eat. A good place to watch "New Orleans Saints" football games on TV (as long as you're not rooting for whoever they're playing against!)

voyage.name: Bar Redux
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri 4PM till close, Sat Sun 2PM till close
voyage.content: Bar Redux is an off the beaten track hidden at the end of the world in the Bywater area of New Orleans. The bar's slogan says it all, "Come as you are.... Stay as you like". The interior is decorated with personal items of music memorabilia and retro pop culture treasures. The Bar's exterior features a unique art mural by Street Artist, Michael Roman. The vintage 1936 red neon BAR sign invites you in. Inside you will

voyage.name: Lookout Inn Bed & Breakfast
voyage.content: A very fashionable B&B with modern, trendy decor and a really attractive, small pool in the courtyard. They play up their "hidden" location's appeal to those who want to stay off the beaten path, and for celebrities who appreciate discretion both on the part of the inn and locals around the area.

voyage.name: Maison de Macarty
voyage.content: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, this 1860s Victorian home features five rooms in the main house, two private cottages, and private bath facilities.

voyage.name: Katrina National Memorial Foundation Museum
voyage.content: Commemorates the natural disaster that struck here.

voyage.name: Fats Domino House
voyage.content: Those wishing to drive by the house of music legend will find it on Caffin St between St. Claude and Claiborne; you can't miss the large letters "F D" on the front.

voyage.name: House of Dance and Feathers
voyage.content: 1317 Tupelo Street. Small museum dedicated to local Mardi Gras Indians and Second Line culture. Curator Ronald W. Lewis has interesting stories. Open by appointment only; contact in advance. Dan Baum's critically acclaimed book, "NIne Lives, Death and Life in New Orleans", which spans the 40 year history between Hurricane Betsy and Katrina, appropriately begins and ends with Ronald Lewis. If you are coming to New Orl

voyage.name: Jackson Barracks Military Museum
voyage.content: Jackson Barracks military base has been here since the 1830s. This is an unorthodox choice for most Lower 9th visitors, but the Louisiana National Guard has an interesting military museum, with artifacts, weapons and memorabilia from every major American war.

voyage.name: Zeitgeist Multi-Disciplinary Arts Center
voyage.content: This is a really cool complex with art films/indie films shown nearly every night. Check the calendar before coming, but mostly just to see what's on—it's a busy, thriving arts complex! On the second Saturday of each month 11AM-4:30PM, Zeitgeist opens the Och Gallery, which always has interesting art exhibits. The store is a great browse too, and is open one hour before nightly events.

voyage.name: Common Ground Relief
voyage.content: Short-term and long-term volunteers stay at one of two buildings

voyage.name: Lafayette Cemetery #1
voyage.hours: Closed to the public until further notice
voyage.content: Historic old cemetery with above ground tombs and distinctive architecture. The cemetery has been featured in many TV shows and movies set in New Orleans.

voyage.name: Latter Branch, New Orleans Public Library
voyage.content: Yes, you can read a book or get a bit of internet time, but this branch of the library is in a 1907 vintage mansion, formerly the home of silent film star Marguerite Clark. This makes it a St. Charles mansion you can see the elegant interior of for free!

voyage.name: Freret Street Market
voyage.content: The first Saturday of most months, featuring produce, crafts, and free live music. Freret Street just upriver from Napoleon Avenue.

voyage.name: Le Bon Temps Roule
voyage.content: Local acts, good beer and burgers. Soul Rebels Brass Band play every Thursday night, it is standing room only and usually packed to the brim so get there early or expect to push your way through a crowd.

voyage.name: The Columns
voyage.content: Old mansion converted into a small hotel. One side of the downstairs front has a bar, the other side a live music venue. Cool jazz and gypsy swing in an elegant setting.

voyage.name: Dos Jefes
voyage.content: Cigar bar; hot modern jazz in a smoky atmosphere.

voyage.name: Neutral Ground Coffee House
voyage.content: Coffee House with more than the usual coffee-house folk singers; eclectic line up can also include blues, Cajun, dixieland combos, bluegrass, jug bands, even Hawaiian music. Live music every night.

voyage.name: Tipitina's
voyage.content: Legendary Uptown music club with great local and national talent. Take bus, cab, or car, but well worth the trouble. "Tip's" has a 2nd location in the French Quarter too, but this is the famous one.

voyage.name: Fleurty Girl
voyage.content: Popular creative New Orleans themed t-shirts.

voyage.name: Perlis
voyage.content: Fine men's clothing. The late Hunter S. Thompson came to town to get a seersucker suit here.

voyage.name: Derby Pottery
voyage.content: Derby Pottery and Tile manufactues the iconic New Orleans Blue and White street tiles in the American style (since 2003) and Belgian style. New Orleans Blue and White street tiles are indigenous pieces of history unique to the city of New Orleans. Beginning in the 1880s the city of New Orleans has embedded letter tiles in city sidewalk intersections identifying the two street names. In the more commercial districts o

voyage.name: Garden District Book Shop
voyage.content: Independent book store specializes in local subjects, and usually has a variety of signed copies of books by local authors. Also a small but select case of rare used books.

voyage.name: Octavia Books
voyage.content: One of the city's top independent bookstores, tucked on an Uptown sidestreet. Often hosts author presentations and signings.

voyage.name: Company Burger
voyage.content: Very high quality hamburgers

voyage.name: Frankie & Johnny's
voyage.content: Local favorite for crawfish. If you're not on a diet, get a side order of the fried bell pepper rings.

voyage.name: Freret Street Po-Boy & Donut Shop
voyage.content: Corner of Valance (halfway between Jefferson and Napoleon Avenues). The name explains it.

voyage.name: Juan's Flying Burrito
voyage.content: Reasonably priced Mexican.

voyage.name: La Divina Gelateria
voyage.content: Excellent Italian style panini sandwiches served from 11AM to 7PM, and they stay open 'til 10PM (F Sa 'til 11PM) serving some amazing gelato.

voyage.name: Magazine Po-Boy Shop
voyage.content: Traditional po-boy sandwiches, plus seafood and vegetarian dishes, breakfast omelettes and burritos.

voyage.name: Mahony's Po-Boy Shop
voyage.content: Po-boys, plus a bar with local draft beer.

voyage.name: Mona's
voyage.content: Middle Eastern. Also has branches in Mid-City and Faubourg Marigny.

voyage.name: Nacho Mama's
voyage.content: Mexican, lunch & dinner 7 days a week.

voyage.name: Nirvana
voyage.content: Awesome $10 buffet every weekday lunch, as well as Thursday and Sunday nights. Great food, good value.

voyage.name: Ray's Uptown
voyage.content: Creole and po-boys. Live music some evenings.

voyage.name: Slice Pizzeria
voyage.content: Slice Pizzeria is one of New Orleans most popular pizzeria's and Italian eateries serving fresh pizzas by the slice and the pie.

voyage.name: Stein's Deli
voyage.content: Great fresh deli sandwiches.

voyage.name: Surrey's Cafe and Juice Bar
voyage.content: Breakfast and lunch, lots of fresh local ingredients.

voyage.name: The Creole Creamery
voyage.content: Truly good ice cream, from a small cup or cone to a huge elaborate sundae. They also make shakes & malts in the old fashioned soda fountain style, and offer many locally made fresh flavors of ice creams, from standard to distinctive, and even a few sugar-free flavors.

voyage.name: La Divina Gelateria
voyage.content: The gelato here costs a little bit more, but it is some of the most amazing you'll have ever tasted. 11AM-9PM; they also serve fresh panini and salads during lunchtime.

voyage.name: Hansen's Sno-Bliz
voyage.content: 4801 Tchopitoulas at Bourdeaux a few blocks up from Napoleon. The Commander's Palace of sno-ball stands; ice shaved microscopically fine, flavored with shockingly luscious syrups made fresh every day. Dozens of flavours to choose from, and you can also add whipped cream, ice cream, condensed milk, marshmallows or crushed pineapple. A local legend since the 1930s! Tu-Su 1PM-7PM, open May 1-Labor Day. If they're not op

voyage.name: St. James Cheese Shop
voyage.content: The staff of knowledgeable cheese mongers will help you fill your cheese needs. They also make tasty lunch sandwiches to eat there or take out.

voyage.name: Sucré
voyage.content: Artisan gelato, cakes, chocolates and pastries prepared daily by an award winning team of pastry chefs.

voyage.name: Tee Eva's
voyage.content: Good sno-balls and tasty pies and praline candy. Try the miniature pies (pecan, sweet-potato, or creole cream cheese), just enough for a snack.

voyage.name: Still Perkin'
voyage.content: In "The Rink", a small shopping center at the corner of Washington Avenue.

voyage.name: Ancora Pizzeria & Salumeria
voyage.content: Upscale pizzeria -- they imported a 3-ton wood-burning oven from Naples. Also makes salumi (Italian style cold cuts). Bar with draft beers, wines, cocktails.

voyage.name: Cafe Atchafalaya
voyage.content: Seafood and decadent desserts. Look for the giant frying pan on the side of the building and get ready for great eats. An established restaurant for over 30 years, the Cafe came back big after hurricane Katrina with a new owner, a beautifully renovated interior, and full menu of New Orleans classics with an original twist. Come early for brunch on the weekend or stay late in the bar every night.

voyage.name: Baru
voyage.content: Caribbean Latin bistro & tapas

voyage.name: Casamento's
voyage.content: Oysters, oysterloaf. A local tradition for generations. Note: This is a cash-only establishment. There is an ATM inside the restaurant.

voyage.name: Crêpe Nanou
voyage.content: Crêpes and other French taste treats, dinner only.

voyage.name: Dick and Jenny's
voyage.content: A casual fine dining contemporary creole restaurant set in a mid-nineteenth century barge board cottage. Reservations are not taken.

voyage.name: High Hat Cafe
voyage.content: Casual Southern and Louisiana Cuisine.

voyage.name: Ignatius
voyage.content: Cajun, Creole and po-boys, lunch and dinner. Try the roast beef po' boy, it is the bomb.

voyage.name: Lilette
voyage.content: New Orleans Magazine Chef of the Year Chef John Harris cooks you an unforgettable meal in this neighborhood bistro.

voyage.name: Martinique Bistro
voyage.content: French Caribbean, dinner.

voyage.name: Mayas
voyage.content: Latin American & Caribbean cuisine, with Cuban predominating. Dinner Tu-Sa; lunch F Sa, brunch Su.

voyage.name: Nirvana
voyage.content: Indian.

voyage.name: La Petit Grocery
voyage.content: An old neighborhood grocery morphed into a fine restaurant. Veal, pork, duck, etc. Dinner M-Sa 6PM-10PM.

voyage.name: Reginelli's
voyage.content: 741 State (at Magazine). Italian & pizza.

voyage.name: Savvy Gourmet
voyage.content: 4519 Magazine, Gourmet food and cooking utensil shop also serves fresh made sadnwiches, salads, and treats at lunch time.

voyage.name: Voodoo BBQ
voyage.content: Trendy barbecue.

voyage.name: Zea
voyage.content: Popular local chain.

voyage.name: Clancy's
voyage.content: Popular and local uptown Contemporary Creole bistro.

voyage.name: Commander's Palace
voyage.content: One of the most highly regarded traditional upscale restaurants.

voyage.name: Emeril's Delmonico
voyage.content: Celebrity chef Emeril Lagasse's third restaurant in town; he bought out the venerable New Orleans Delmonico's.

voyage.name: Gautreau's
voyage.content: Excellent uptown restaurant!

voyage.name: The Bulldog
voyage.hours: Mon Tue 2PM-2AM, Wed Thu Sun noon-2AM, Fri Sat noon-3AM
voyage.content: One of the city's largest selections of beers on tap and in bottles, also serves burgers and delicious waffle fries.

voyage.name: The Club Ms Mae's
voyage.content: Friendly dive. Cheap! $1 drinks all the time ($2 doubles!)

voyage.name: The Columns
voyage.content: Very classy (but not high-hat)! Has nice patio overlooking St. Charles Avenue. Free food during Friday happy hour from 5PM-7PM. Small combos play live music many evenings.

voyage.name: Cure
voyage.content: Upscale cocktail bar in an out-of the way neighborhood; also serves gourmet small plates. Not cheap, but obsessively high quality.

voyage.name: F & M Patio Bar
voyage.hours: Sun-Thu 7PM-4AM, Fri Sat 7PM-5:30AM. May be open later than posted closing times
voyage.content: A favorite local dive famous for dancing on the pool table.

voyage.name: Fat Harry's
voyage.content: College bar with typical bar food.

voyage.name: Half Moon
voyage.content: Laid back dive. Lots of locals. People like to bring their dogs here.

voyage.name: Igor's Lounge and Game Room
voyage.content: Drink and have a burger while playing the slot machines or doing your laundry in their coin operated machines.

voyage.name: King Pin
voyage.content: Nice laid back bar. Mostly locals. Shuffleboard!

voyage.name: Milan Lounge
voyage.content: Little neighborhood bar. Very friendly bartenders. Chicago Cubs memorabilia all over the place.

voyage.name: Parasol's
voyage.content: Old Irish neighborhood bar. Also serves po-boys and seafood. Their block party on St. Patrick's Day is always jammed.

voyage.name: The Saint
voyage.content: Hipster dive.

voyage.name: St. Joe's Bar
voyage.content: Just an off-beat little bar that knows how to make good drinks. For something different on hot summer days, try the blueberry mojito.

voyage.name: Auberge NOLA
voyage.content: Hostel offers mixed dorms, female-only dorms, and one private apartment with its own bathroom and kitchen. Security lockers provided in dorms. Dorm guests from abroad must provide a foreign passport; American dorm guests need an out-of-state ID and a student ID. Dorms restricted to guests under 40 years of age. Apartment guests need an out-of-state ID or foreign passport and can be of any age. Office open 8:30AM-10PM

voyage.name: Marquette House
voyage.content: A block from the St. Charles Streetcar line (Jackson Street stop), features free but slow Wifi, free parking. The place is not clean and the kitchen has two microwaves but no stoves, cutlery or crockery. There is no TV room or lounge area.

voyage.name: The Quisby
voyage.content: Hostel housed in the former Audubon Hotel, offering both dorms and private rooms. All rooms have ensuite bathrooms. Free wifi and free breakfast included. Full bar on site.

voyage.name: Quality Inn Maison St. Charles
voyage.content: On the streetcar line in the lower part of Uptown, an easy walk from several restaurants.

voyage.name: Southern Comfort Bed and Breakfast
voyage.content: 2 blocks from the St. Charles Avenue Streetcar line and minutes from the French Quarter.

voyage.name: Creole Gardens Bed and Breakfast Inn
voyage.content: One block from the St. Charles Ave. Streetcar Line. Next to the Warehouse District, and 12 blocks from the French Quarter. Famous for colorful banana courtyard, kid and pet friendly and great hot breakfast.

voyage.name: Hotel Saint Vincent
voyage.content: It was built in 1861, and restored and reimagined in 2021, the 75-room Hotel Saint Vincent sits on the corner of Magazine and Race streets in the Lower Garden District of New Orleans.

voyage.name: Columns Hotel
voyage.content: Small elegant hotel in a Victorian mansion. Also has a great bar and live music downstairs.

voyage.name: Grand Victorian Bed & Breakfast
voyage.content: Historic bed and breakfast in the Garden District. Complimentary breakfast, private baths, free wi-fi, steps to the street car

voyage.name: Hotel Indigo New Orleans Garden District
voyage.content: This hotel is on the Mardi Gras parade route. Rooms from $159.

voyage.name: The Green House Inn
voyage.content: A pet friendly, adults only inn featuring a clothing optional swimming pool/spa set in a tropical garden. Amenities include self-serve Continental breakfast, free WiFi, and one free, gated off-street parking space per guest.

voyage.name: Audubon Park
voyage.content: Pleasant park to walk around, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the same fellow who designed Central Park in New York City. Runs from St. Charles Avenue to the river.

voyage.name: Audubon Zoo
voyage.content: Very good zoo, see the rare white alligators, at the upper end of Magazine Street. Riverboats connect the Zoo to the Central Business District; also accessible from the St. Charles Streetcar via a shuttle bus that runs back and forth from the main entrance to Audubon Park on St. Charles to the Zoo.

voyage.name: Cascade Stables
voyage.content: Horse stables, riding lessons.

voyage.name: Tulane University
voyage.content: The main campus of New Orleans' most famous university stretches from St. Charles Avenue across from Audubon Park back to Claiborne Avenue. It includes a few attractions of special interest to some:

voyage.name: Tulane Jazz Archive
voyage.content: New Orleans jazz fans can see a display of photographs and artifacts, and research by reading or listening to interviews with historic jazz musicians.

voyage.name: Middle American Research Institute
voyage.content: With a major renovation of Dinwiddie Hall being completed, the pre-Columbian artifacts are not on public display at writing but will return in 2012. However a few items are on display elsewhere on campus, and the Institute sponsors special events. Lovers of ancient Meso-America should check the website for details.

voyage.name: Uptown Crescent City Farmers Market
voyage.content: Market with fresh produce and fresh prepared local dishes. Every Tuesday 9AM-1PM, University Square parking lot (formerly known as Uptown Square), 200 block of Broadway, near the riverfront, a couple blocks on the upriver side of Audubon Park.

voyage.name: Campus Connection
voyage.content: University, fraternity & sorority related merchandise

voyage.name: Elio's Wine Warehouse
voyage.content: Good selection of wine, liquor, and beer.

voyage.name: Mushroom
voyage.content: New and used records; posters, t-shirts, and assorted paraphernalia.

voyage.name: Crepes à la Carte
voyage.content: Fresh made sweet or savory crepes for a meal or snack. Has a small bench and when the weather is good a couple of little outdoor tables, but most business is "to go"; the crepes come in a convenient paper cone so they can be eaten while walking.

voyage.name: Felipe's Taqueria
voyage.content: Popular location of small chain; fresh made Mexican

voyage.name: Café Freret
voyage.content: Tables are shaded under a roof but not walled in. "Pet friendly" if you're looking for a place to eat with your dog. Prices reasonable, though service can be slow.

voyage.name: Naked Pizza
voyage.content: Pizza with all natural healthy ingredients; even vegan and gluten free options. The original location of what has become a growing franchise. Take out or delivery.

voyage.name: Pyramids Cafe
voyage.content: Middle Eastern. Eat in or delivery.

voyage.name: Ted's Frostop
voyage.content: Old school style burgers, shakes, fries & rootbeer. Also simple breakfasts.

voyage.name: Wing Zone
voyage.content: Branch of chain, chicken wings, chicken fingers, burgers

voyage.name: Kupcake Factory
voyage.content: Cupcakes and gelato

voyage.name: First Cup Cafe
voyage.content: Nice small coffee house, free Wi-Fi for paying customers.

voyage.name: PJ's Coffee & Tea
voyage.content: 2 locations of popular local chain on the Tulane campus; 6501 Willow (Willow Hall); and in the breezeway of Stern Hall on Freret at McAlister.

voyage.name: Audubon Clubhouse Cafe
voyage.address: 6500 Magazine St, on Golf Club Drive
voyage.content: Old clubhouse is open to the public for breakfast, lunch, and Sunday brunch. The reason to come here is for the relaxing view of the park and golf course; sit on the porch having a leisurely meal while sipping mimosas or bloody marys.

voyage.name: Tartine
voyage.content: French style bakery & cafe; breakfast & lunch. Also has fresh baguettes, scones, etc to go for a tasty picnic in the nearby Audubon Park.

voyage.name: The Boot
voyage.content: A favorite University District bar for decades. Also has a grill serving bar food and a small convenience store attached.

voyage.name: Felipe's
voyage.content: Mexican restaurant listed at "eat" above has a nice bar, with frozen margaritas and Mexican beer on tap in addition to standard bar drinks. Unlike most New Orleans bars, not open late.

voyage.name: The Palms
voyage.content: Bar & grill, mostly University clientele

voyage.name: Robert's Bar & Liquor Store
voyage.content: Old neighborhood smoky dive bar; pool table and ping-pong table.

voyage.name: Park View Guest House
voyage.content: Beautiful historic guest house that was built for visitors to the 1884 World's Fair. The side yard is Audubon Park and the streetcar stops right outside, hard to beat the location.
